overview.summary: Fission-based electricity — among the lowest-carbon, lowest-death sources, in a debate that scrambles partisan lines.
overview.scope_covered: Civilian fission for grid power: cost, safety, waste, the climate case.
overview.why_now: A shrinking fleet is turning a corner: AI power deals and eased US licensing point to ~15 new reactors online in 2026, with China's first commercial SMR close behind.

stats.label: Deaths per TWh · lifecycle
stats.note: Among the safest sources measured by lifecycle deaths per unit of electricity — on par with wind and solar, far below coal (24.6) and gas (2.8).

stats.label: Share of global power
stats.note: Nuclear has held steady at about 9% of world electricity for a decade, even as China's output has overtaken France's.

stats.label: Capacity factor
stats.note: The global fleet hit a record 83% capacity factor in 2024 — still tops among power sources; the US fleet alone runs near 92%.

stats.label: Lifecycle CO₂ · g/kWh
stats.note: About 12 grams of CO2 per kWh across its full lifecycle — on par with wind, roughly 40x below gas and 70x below coal.

stats.label: Build cost · West vs Korea
stats.note: Recent Western builds like Vogtle and Hinkley Point have cost roughly four times as much per kilowatt as comparable Korean projects.

stats.label: High-level waste, all-time
stats.note: Every gram of high-level waste ever produced worldwide would cover one football field just a few metres deep.

stats.label: Operating reactors worldwide
stats.note: About 438 power reactors run across roughly 30 countries, with another 80 under construction — over half of them in China.

stats.label: Average reactor age
stats.note: The global fleet averages about 32 years old; most reactors are licensed for 40 but routinely extended to 60, and now sometimes 80.

questions.text: Are runaway Western nuclear costs fixable, or structural?
questions.why: South Korea's government confirmed in January 2026 it will build two more large reactors, continuing a track record of roughly a quarter the per-kW cost of recent Western projects — while Plant Vogtle, two years after completion at over $36.8bn, remains the cautionary tale and still no US utility has ordered a repeat AP1000. If the gap is lost supply chain and workforce, standardised repeat-building fixes it; if it's the safety review, litigation and financing that Western practice bakes in, reform won't.

questions.text: Is the AI-driven nuclear "restart boom" delivering real power, or running into reality?
questions.why: Data-center demand pushed Constellation and Holtec to restart shuttered plants — Three Mile Island and Palisades — on the strength of 20-year corporate power deals with Microsoft and others, and DOE has backed $17.5bn in loans for ten new large reactors. But Three Mile Island's grid reconnection has reportedly slipped toward 2031 on transmission bottlenecks, critics point to NRC staff departures and reactor-vessel embrittlement risk, and skeptics call the whole restart wave a PR-driven bet ahead of the engineering. Whether this is a genuine inflection point or hype outrunning delivery is unresolved.

questions.text: Is the waste problem solved in principle, but unsolved in practice?
questions.why: Deep geological disposal is mature engineering, but even Finland's pioneering Onkalo repository — after successful trial encapsulations — is still awaiting its operating license and first real spent-fuel shipment, expected late 2026 or 2027, not yet actually operating as sometimes reported. Sweden only broke ground on a second repository in 2025, decades behind Finland, and France's Cigéo remains years from operating. Almost everywhere else the barrier is political siting, not physics or engineering.

questions.text: Should ageing reactors be extended, restarted, or replaced with new build?
questions.why: Life-extension to 80 years is now routine and the cheapest firm low-carbon power available, and AI-driven demand has opened a third path — restarting recently shuttered plants like Three Mile Island and Palisades under corporate power deals. But restarts carry their own cost and schedule risk (Three Mile Island's reconnection has slipped toward 2031), and neither extending nor restarting rebuilds the construction workforce and supply chain a real new-build fleet would need.

questions.text: Are small modular reactors a breakthrough or overhyped?
questions.why: China's Linglong One became the first land-based SMR to reach commercial operation in 2026, while Western designs — the BWRX-300 at Darlington, TerraPower's Natrium — remain under construction or licensing, constrained by a bottlenecked HALEU fuel supply chain. Whether Western SMRs can replicate China's lead, and whether shrinking a reactor forfeits the economies of scale that favoured large plants, is still open.

questions.text: Is public fear of nuclear the real barrier, not its actual risk?
questions.why: US favorability hit a record 77% in 2026 (a roughly 6-to-1 ratio of strong support to strong opposition), and 70% would accept a new small reactor next to their existing local plant — evidence the safety-record/perception gap may be closing nationally even as local waste-site and new-build opposition persists. Whether remaining resistance reflects outsized dread or legitimate risk-and-consent concerns stays contested.

positions.name: Climate Pragmatist
positions.steelman: The only zero-carbon source already proven to run a grid around the clock at scale - and the climate clock is too tight to take it off the table.
positions.description: Nuclear is the only dispatchable, zero-carbon power proven at national scale: France still runs close to 70% of its grid on nuclear (electricity there is now about 95% low-carbon), and reactors deliver firm output around the clock at capacity factors above 90%. IPCC mitigation pathways lean on expanding it, and the AI-driven surge in electricity demand - which has pushed Microsoft, Google, Amazon and Meta into direct nuclear power-purchase deals since 2024 - is now testing in real time whether renewables alone can meet a fast-growing grid on schedule.
positions.proponents: James Hansen, Stewart Brand, Clean Air Task Force
positions.representative_note: climate scientist who broke with much of the green movement to back nuclear.

positions.name: Cost Skeptic
positions.steelman: Climate is a race against time, and slow, over-budget reactors buy less carbon abatement per dollar, and far later, than renewables we can build today.
positions.description: Vogtle ran about seven years late and tens of billions over budget; Hinkley Point C is now delayed to 2030 - eight-plus years behind schedule - with costs risen to roughly £49 billion against an original £18 billion, and EDF booked a further €2.5 billion writedown on it in February 2026 alone. Meanwhile BNEF's 2026 benchmark put battery storage at a record-low $78/MWh, and Amory Lovins notes the world added more renewable capacity in the first half of 2025 than nuclear has added in decades - nuclear has never shown the falling-cost curve renewables have.
positions.proponents: Amory Lovins, BNEF analysts, Mark Z. Jacobson
positions.representative_note: physicist and advocate of the efficiency-and-renewables path.

positions.name: New-Nuclear Advocate
positions.steelman: Stop building bespoke megaprojects: freeze one design, build it in series - and factory-built reactors are now literally under construction, bankrolled by Big Tech's AI power crunch.
positions.description: Small modular and Gen-IV reactors aim to replace one-off gigawatt megaprojects with standardised, factory-built units installed in series - and in 2026 that bet moved from paper to concrete. TerraPower's Natrium plant won the first-ever NRC construction permit for a non-light-water commercial reactor and broke ground; NuScale's uprated design cleared NRC review. Meta has committed up to 6.6 GW across TerraPower Natrium, Oklo Aurora and utility deals, Amazon backs X-energy, and Google has contracted Kairos Power - all racing to power AI data centres on the premise that serial, factory-built nuclear can now be bought at scale.
positions.representative_note: Gen-IV developer whose Natrium design broke ground in 2026 after winning the first NRC construction permit for a non-light-water reactor.

positions.name: Risk-First Skeptic
positions.steelman: Some risks - meltdowns, proliferation, waste outlasting civilisation - are too catastrophic and irreversible to accept when safer options now exist, especially as licensing gets rushed.
positions.description: Meltdowns, weapons proliferation and waste that stays dangerous for tens of thousands of years are not ordinary, insurable risks - they are low-probability, high-consequence hazards that outlast the institutions meant to contain them. Chernobyl and Fukushima displaced whole regions for years. Critics now also point to 2025's push to compress NRC licensing reviews to 18 months and fast-track advanced-reactor approval as exactly the kind of shortcut that has preceded past accidents, while a decentralised renewable grid fails gracefully and locally.
positions.proponents: Naomi Oreskes, Union of Concerned Scientists, anti-nuclear NGOs
positions.representative_note: historian of science writing on risk and trust.

positions.name: Go all-in: a fast, standardised build-out
positions.steelman: Firm, clean power at scale is non-negotiable for deep decarbonisation — commit to one design and build it relentlessly until costs fall.
positions.description: Treat nuclear as essential baseload for a net-zero grid and fix the cost problem the way Korea did: one standard design, a steady pipeline, and an intact workforce and supply chain. This is no longer theoretical - US executive orders signed in May 2025 aim to quadruple nuclear capacity to 400 GW by 2050 with 10 new large reactors under construction by 2030, France has committed roughly €89 billion to six standardised EPR2 units, and Korea continues exporting its serially-built APR-1400 fleet abroad.

positions.name: Keep existing plants, bet new money on renewables
positions.steelman: Every dollar should buy the most carbon abatement per year — and right now that's overwhelmingly solar, wind and storage, not slow, costly new reactors.
positions.description: Extend safe existing reactors for their cheap firm power - as seen in Diablo Canyon's life extension and the Three Mile Island and Palisades restarts - but direct new investment to renewables and storage, which deploy faster and, on a multi-year view, cheaper per tonne of CO2 avoided. Global battery storage costs hit a record low of $78/MWh in 2025 even as solar and wind costs ticked up that year on supply-chain constraints, a reminder that the renewables cost story is still trending down overall but no longer perfectly smooth.

crux.lead: Is the West's nuclear cost problem one we can engineer away — or one we've chosen?
crux.subtitle: Almost everyone agrees nuclear is low-carbon and historically safe. The real split is narrower: whether runaway Western build costs are a fixable industrial failure or the deliberate price of democratic caution about catastrophic risk.
crux.empirical: Then the cost gap is contingent, not intrinsic — the residue of lost supply chains, first-of-a-kind designs, and stop-start programs. Korea still builds at a fraction of Western cost, and France once did by repeating one standardized reactor. And the test is finally live: with the first factory-built reactors now under construction, the learning-curve bet is about to meet real cost data — evidence and execution could settle it.
crux.values: Then the high price isn't failure but caution made visible — the safety margins, licensing rigor, and veto points a democracy chose against meltdown, proliferation, and waste outlasting its institutions. On this view, today's rush to speed up licensing doesn't settle the argument; it just remakes the choice. Building cheaper means caring less — and no data can close that gap. Only a choice can.

Cross-partisan framing still holds — if anything sharper: a Republican administration is now the one pushing hardest (May 2025 nuclear executive orders, NRC fast-track rules), while climate-motivated Democrats and tech hyperscalers also back it. No change needed.
Cost, safety, waste, and the climate case remain exactly the live sub-debates (SMR economics, Part 53 licensing/safety tradeoffs, uranium supply); scope still fits without expansion.
Weapons, fusion, and naval propulsion remain correctly out of scope; no crossover developments found that would require pulling them in.

Old → new: 'A retiring fleet meets climbing demand from AI and electrification, just as climate targets need firm clean power.' → 'A shrinking fleet is turning a corner: AI power deals and eased US licensing point to ~15 new reactors online in 2026, with China's first commercial SMR close behind.' Reason: the 'retiring fleet' framing is now stale — 2025 saw the fleet actually shrink (7 shutdowns vs 2 additions, net -1.1 GW per BloombergNEF), but 2026 is forecast to add ~15 reactors (~12 GW), the industry's biggest rebound in years, driven by hyperscaler power deals (Meta/Oklo Ohio campus, AWS/Talen Susquehanna PPA), the US NRC's new Part 53 licensing framework (effective April 29, 2026) plus May 2025 executive orders, the first-ever restart of a decommissioned US plant (Palisades), and China's Linglong One targeting the world's first commercial land-based SMR in 2026.

No facts introduced beyond those already in the updated positions.

verdicts.critic:
Neutrality review of the refreshed Nuclear Energy draft. I checked each section for tilt, house verdicts, strawmanning, and false balance.

Overall: the draft handles asymmetry the way the editorial rules prescribe — the pro-leaning weight is carried by shared, sourced Basics facts (deaths/TWh, lifecycle CO2) and by prevalence weights, not by editorial voice. The Crux is the strongest neutrality asset here: the values branch gives the risk-first worldview full force ("Building cheaper means caring less — and no data can close that gap. Only a choice can.") rather than treating caution as an obstacle, and the empirical branch is equally live. No section delivers a house verdict.

Position parity: all six positions read as genuine steelmen a proponent would endorse. The Cost Skeptic gets concrete, current ammunition (Hinkley to £49bn, EDF's €2.5bn writedown, $78/MWh storage); the Risk-First Skeptic gets a structural argument (uninsurable tail risk, institutions outlasted by waste, 2025 licensing compression as a live grievance) rather than a caricature of fear. The questions section consistently presents both readings (restart boom "genuine inflection point or hype outrunning delivery"; costs "fixable or structural"). Actions are balanced: one donate option per side of the cost/renewables split, plus a risk-first-aligned local action.

No major position is missing: hard phase-out opposition is subsumed by the Risk-First Skeleton's "too catastrophic to accept when safer options now exist," and the two bracket positions cover the policy split. Prevalence weights (87/74/70/52/18/10) are plausible given 2026 US favorability data and are the correct mechanism for honest non-balance.

Residual lean is minor and non-misleading: the Basics stat mix runs favorable (5 of 8 flatter nuclear, 1 unflattering), the waste stat borrows the industry's "football field" framing from a WNA page literally titled "myths and realities," and one question title ("Is public fear the real barrier, not its actual risk?") presupposes the pro-side answer before its why-text restores balance. These are polish items, not distortions — the con-side facts that matter (4x cost gap, Vogtle, delays, unresolved siting) are present and prominent. Pass.
notes: Basics stat mix leans favorable (deaths, capacity factor, CO2, waste-volume, plus neutral counts) with only the West-vs-Korea cost stat carrying the con side. Consider adding one durable con-side stat — e.g. median Western construction-time overrun or years-since-last-on-time Western build — so the shared-facts layer carries the asymmetry in both directions.

The high-level waste stat uses the industry's signature minimizing frame ("one football field just a few metres deep") sourced to WNA's advocacy-titled "myths and realities" page. The number is fine; consider a flatter phrasing ("~400 kt total, all-time") and/or an IAEA source so the framing isn't borrowed from one side's talking point.

5 of 8 Basics stats cite the World Nuclear Association (an industry body). Where equivalents exist — reactor counts and under-construction figures via IAEA PRIS — prefer the official source per the sourcing hierarchy.

Question title "Is public fear of nuclear the real barrier, not its actual risk?" presupposes the pro-nuclear answer; the why-text recovers balance ("legitimate risk-and-consent concerns stays contested"), but a symmetric title like "Is the barrier to nuclear public dread — or unresolved consent?" would avoid the tilt at the headline level.

Crux subtitle asserts "Almost everyone agrees nuclear is... historically safe" — risk-first proponents would quibble that measured death rates and safety-against-tail-risk are different claims. "historically low-death" would be airtight; the values branch already honors their real objection.

The two bracket positions (Go all-in; Keep existing, bet on renewables) have empty proponents/representative fields while the four analytic positions are fully attributed. Symmetric between the two brackets, so not misleading — but populating both (e.g. France/DOE vs. IEEFA/Germany's path) would match the rigor of the rest.
Several steelmen exceed the ~90-char banner target (Cost Skeptic ~140, Risk-First ~160) — a distill issue, not a neutrality one, flagged in passing.

All four analytical positions read as genuine strongest cases a proponent would endorse: Climate Pragmatist gets the firm-power + climate-clock argument, Cost Skeptic gets the Lovins opportunity-cost-per-dollar frame (not a caricatured 'nuclear bad'), New-Nuclear Advocate gets the serial-manufacturing thesis with 2026 groundbreaking proof points, and Risk-First Skeptic gets the low-probability/high-consequence + institutional-longevity argument plus the current licensing-rush hook — no side is softened or strawmanned.

Steelman lines run ~150-185 chars against the ~90-char banner guideline. Each could be distilled without losing force, e.g. Risk-First: 'Meltdowns, proliferation, waste outlasting civilisation — some risks are too irreversible to accept when safer options exist.' Climate Pragmatist: 'The only zero-carbon source proven to run a grid around the clock — and the climate clock is too tight to drop it.'

Internal inconsistency on the battery-storage figure: Cost Skeptic's description calls $78/MWh 'BNEF's 2026 benchmark' while position 6 dates the same record-low figure to 2025. One year must be wrong — reconcile against the actual BNEF release date (an accuracy-pass item, flagged here because it sits inside two position descriptions).

The stance layer (positions 5-6) offers 'go all-in' and 'keep existing, build renewables' but no phase-out/no-extension stance, so a Risk-First proponent has no home on the what-to-do axis — position 6 explicitly endorses life extensions no Greenpeace-type advocate would sign. Defensible on prevalence grounds (the phase-out stance's real-world weight has cratered since 2023-24, and asymmetry is meant to be carried by prevalence), but worth a deliberate decision rather than an omission.

Crux subtitle's 'almost everyone agrees nuclear is low-carbon and historically safe' slightly over-concedes for the Risk-First camp, whose claim is about unrealized tail risk rather than the historical record — the values branch immediately restores their frame ('caution made visible', 'building cheaper means caring less'), so it does not mislead, but 'historically safe' could become 'has a strong historical safety record' to keep the tail-risk distinction open.
Punctuation drift: positions 1-4 steelmans use hyphens where 5-6 use em-dashes; normalize to the house em-dash.

blocking.issue: Questions[4] (SMRs) states as fact that "China's Linglong One became the first land-based SMR to reach commercial operation in 2026." This is not verified: as of the latest IAEA PRIS data (May 2026) Linglong One has no recorded first criticality, grid connection, or commercial operation — it completed cold testing (Oct 2025) and a non-nuclear turbine test (Dec 2025/Jan 2026) and is targeting commercial operation in 2026. It also contradicts the draft's own why_now line ("China's first commercial SMR close behind").
blocking.fix: Rephrase to prospective: e.g. "China's Linglong One is in final commissioning and slated to become the first land-based SMR in commercial operation in 2026, while Western designs… remain under construction or licensing." This also restores internal consistency with why_now.

blocking.issue: The Three Mile Island "slipped toward 2031" claim (Questions[1] and Questions[3]) is stale: PJM's 2031 transmission timeline was reported in March 2026, but FERC granted Constellation's waiver on 5 June 2026 to transfer ~760 MW of Eddystone interconnection rights to Crane, putting the restart back on the 2027 target. Questions[3] states the slip flatly ("has slipped toward 2031"); Questions[1] hedges with "reportedly" but still presents it as the current state.
blocking.fix: Update both: e.g. "PJM told Constellation grid reconnection could slip to 2031 on transmission bottlenecks before a June 2026 FERC waiver restored the 2027 target" — which still supports the point that restarts carry grid/schedule risk while reflecting the resolution.

blocking.issue: Basics stat "Operating reactors worldwide" note says the ~80 reactors under construction are "over half of them in China." China has roughly 36–37 units under construction — about 45–50% of the 74–80 total depending on source, and ~45% against the cited WNA database's own count of 80. "Over half" is wrong versus the cited source (IEA/EIA put China at half of under-construction capacity, not over half of units).
blocking.fix: Change to "nearly half of them in China" (or "about half"). The WNA dashboard figures of 438 operable and 80 under construction otherwise match the draft exactly.

notes: Cost Skeptic says Hinkley Point C is "eight-plus years behind schedule" — no published baseline yields 8: it is ~5 years behind the 2016 FID target (2025), ~7 behind the 2023 date assumed in the 2013 strike-price deal, ~13 behind the original 2017 promise. Suggest "at least five years behind its investment-decision schedule" or anchor the baseline. The €2.5bn EDF charge (Feb 2026), the 2030 first-power date, and the ~£49bn today's-prices figure all check out.

Capacity-factor stat says the fleet "hit a record 83% capacity factor in 2024"; WNA's Performance Report 2025 reports 83% (up from 82%) and calls 2024 a record for generation (2,667 TWh), not explicitly a record capacity factor. Safer: "83% in 2024 — higher than any other power source."

High-level-waste stat: the cited WNA myths page supports the ~400,000 t used-fuel figure but does not contain the football-field comparison; the arithmetic (~40,000 m³ ≈ a few metres over a pitch) is defensible, but consider a source that actually makes the comparison or rephrase around the 400 kt figure alone.

France EPR2 "roughly €89 billion": EDF's official Dec 2025 estimate is €72.8bn in 2020 prices, ≈€89bn in 2025 prices. Accurate as written, but citing "€72.8bn (2020 prices; ~€89bn today)" would match the headline number readers will encounter.

Questions[1] attributes both restarts to "20-year corporate power deals with Microsoft and others"; Microsoft's deal is TMI-specific — Palisades runs on co-op PPAs (Wolverine/Hoosier) plus a DOE loan. Consider tightening to avoid implying Palisades is a Big Tech deal.

The 77% favorability / 70% SMR-acceptance figures are confirmed from Bisconti Research's 2026 survey; note Bisconti is industry-associated and general polls (Gallup/Pew) run nearer 60%, so "record 77%" is source-specific — fine, but attribution in the deep layer would strengthen it.

Verified and current: DOE $17.5bn loans for 10 AP1000s (announced 23 June 2026), Natrium NRC construction permit (4 March 2026, first commercial non-LWR permit in over 40 years), Meta up-to-6.6 GW deals with Oklo/TerraPower/Vistra (Jan 2026), BNEF $78/MWh 4-hour BESS benchmark for 2025, Korea's Jan 2026 confirmation of two reactors, BNEF's ~15 reactors expected online in 2026, Vogtle $36.8bn, Onkalo licence pending with first disposal expected late 2026/2027, regulations.gov docket NRC-2025-0975 (reactor licensing modernization proposed rule, issued 1 July 2026), and OWID death rates (0.03 nuclear vs 24.6 coal, 2.8 gas).

The crux is a genuine narrowing, not false balance: it concedes the shared ground explicitly (low-carbon, historically safe — both backed by the Basics stats) and locates the live disagreement at a specific fork: is the Western cost premium a contingent industrial failure (empirically testable, and the draft names the live test — serial factory-built reactors now under construction) or the deliberate price of democratic caution about catastrophic risk (a values choice no data closes). No house verdict is stated; each branch is written so its own proponents would endorse it, and neither branch is given rhetorical victory — the empirical branch gets 'evidence could settle it', the values branch gets 'only a choice can'.

The fork maps cleanly onto the position landscape: the empirical branch is the Climate Pragmatist / New-Nuclear vs Cost Skeptic dispute; the values branch carries the Risk-First Skeptic's actual objection (irreversible tail risk, licensing speed-up as remaking the choice) rather than reducing them to NIMBYism. This is the strongest sign it narrows to where disagreement actually sits.

Minor phrasing risk, not blocking: 'Building cheaper means caring less' is a hard compression that a values-side proponent might soften to something like 'cutting the margins is choosing to accept more risk' — the current line flirts with sounding like the other side's caricature of them, though the 'On this view' framing keeps it inside the steelman. Worth a phrasing pass if editing anyway.

The empirical branch's 'the test is finally live' echoes industry framing slightly; it stays neutral because the draft elsewhere (restart-boom question, TMI slip to 2031, NRC staffing critiques) supplies the skeptical counterweight, so the crux is not carrying a tilt on its own. Optionally, one clause acknowledging the test could also come back negative would make the symmetry airtight.

Scope note, non-blocking: the crux deliberately routes waste, SMR, and restart disputes through the cost/caution fork rather than treating them as separate cruxes. That is a defensible editorial narrowing — waste siting and licensing speed are themselves instances of the 'caution as chosen cost' branch — and the questions section carries the remainder.
